source: Fischhoff, Slovic, Lichtenstein (1978) Fault trees: sensitivity of estimated failure probabilities to problem representation. Exp 1
finding: People shown a car-won't-start fault tree with branches deleted did not move the missing causes into 'all other problems'. They treated the listed branches as nearly complete (out of sight, out of mind).
numbers: Unpruned tree n=93; pruned tree 1 n=29; pruned tree 2 n=26. 'Other' should have risen about six-fold (.078 to .468) but only about doubled. Only 1 of 55 pruned-tree subjects gave 'other' a large enough share. Read-aloud vs self-paced made no difference (mean abs diff .018).
limits: University of Oregon students, one domain (car starting). Availability account beat the credibility account, but some sensitivity to omissions was shown ('other' larger than in unpruned group, p<.001).
agent_relevance: A scaffold that lists a fixed hypothesis set will make the model act as if the list is complete. The agent needs an explicit 'what is not on this list' step and should not trust its own list for coverage.

source: Fischhoff, Slovic, Lichtenstein (1978) Fault trees, Exp 2 (focus on 'all other problems')
finding: Telling subjects to focus on the 'all other problems' branch helped only partly. It raised the 'other' share of pruned-tree groups by about 50 percent but it stayed far below the right level.
numbers: 82 subjects. Pruned group 1 'other' .140 to .217; pruned group 2 .227 to .346 (t about 1.8 each). Unpruned group 'other' .067 vs .078 in Exp 1 (no change).
limits: Marginal significance (t about 1.8). A prompt-style 'look at what is missing' is a weak fix, not a cure.
agent_relevance: A generic 'consider other causes' prompt will under-correct. Expect a partial effect only; pair it with a concrete method (see b17, b19).

source: Fischhoff, Slovic, Lichtenstein (1978) Fault trees, Exp 6 with experienced mechanics
finding: The omission blindness replicated in experienced mechanics. Experience and self-rated knowledge did not predict who noticed what was missing.
numbers: 29 of 60 mailed questionnaires returned (16 pruned, 13 unpruned). Deleted branches plus 'other' should be .441; pruned-tree mechanics gave .215 (median .47 expected vs .16 observed; U z=2.87). Years of experience vs 'other' share: tau=.058. Experience ranged 2 to 43 years.
limits: Small N, 48 percent response rate, self-selected mechanics.
agent_relevance: Expertise does not remove the gap in knowing what has not been listed. Do not assume a stronger model fixes completeness.

source: Fischhoff, Slovic, Lichtenstein (1978) Fault trees, Exp 5 (splitting and fusing branches)
finding: The same set of causes got more weight when shown as two branches than as one. How hypotheses are grouped changes how likely they feel.
numbers: N=115, one tree each. Split sets got about a third more share (mean +.066). Sign tests: 20 of 27 (p=.010) and 19 of 26 (p=.014) for the two splits; fused: 24 of 33 (p=.007).
limits: Grouping chosen by the experimenters. The response scale floor (.01) may add to the effect.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis lists in a schema have partition effects. Prefer mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive groups at an even grain.

source: Thomas, Dougherty, Buttaccio (2014) Memory constraints on hypothesis generation and decision making (Current Directions in Psychological Science)
finding: Review of the HyGene account: hypotheses are retrieved from memory, held in working memory, and compared. Only hypotheses held in working memory shape probability judgment and information search. Fewer held hypotheses give higher probability per hypothesis (subadditivity).
numbers: No new data. Cites Dougherty and Hunter 2003a,b for the link of subadditivity with working memory capacity, Thomas et al. 2008 (Psychological Review 115) for the model, Sprenger et al. 2011 for load effects. Model runs used capacity values 2 (low) vs 4 (high).
limits: Review by the model's own authors. Simulations use assumed capacity values, not measured counts of hypotheses in clinicians.
agent_relevance: Maps onto an LLM: the context holds only what was written out. If no alternatives are written, the model judges as if none exist.

source: Thomas, Lange, Dougherty (unpublished, as cited in Thomas et al. 2014) one vs two hypotheses and test choice
finding: Hypothesis count drives test choice. With one hypothesis tied to the symptom, people chose confirming tests. With two, they chose diagnostic tests.
numbers: Learning phase then test selection. No N or effect size given in the review.
limits: Second-hand, no numbers. Dougherty et al. 2010 and Navarro and Perfors 2011 argue confirmatory search can be reasonable in realistic domains.
agent_relevance: Make the agent hold at least two live hypotheses before it picks a test: no test without a rival.

source: Sprenger et al. (2011) Implications of cognitive load for hypothesis generation and probability judgment (Frontiers in Psychology 2:129)
finding: Cognitive load during judgment raised summed probabilities (fewer alternatives compared). Load during encoding also raised judgments, which the model had not predicted.
numbers: Exp 1 N=167, load 1/4/6/8 letters, F(3,161)=3.13 p<.05, sums 261.8/265.4/264.7/271.5 (about 3.7 percent rise; text says about 10). Exp 2 N=73 finger-tapping, F(1,69)=5.56, 177.10 vs 192.02. Exp 3 N=101, F(1,97)=6.55. Working memory span vs sums r=-.187 to -.284 (Exp 1), -.229 to -.476 (Exp 3).
limits: No effect sizes reported. Irrelevant-alternative strength in Exp 2 was confounded (2 vs 8 alternatives). Exp 1 effect is small.
agent_relevance: Overconfidence works through how many alternatives are generated. For an LLM, the count of written alternatives is a measurable proxy.

source: Sprenger et al. (2011) mediation by number of hypotheses recalled
finding: Divided attention at encoding cut the number of alternatives recalled. Controlling for that count removed the effect on judgment, so number generated mediated the bias.
numbers: Exp 3: recalled count by attention F(1,97)=35.07 p<.01. Count vs judgment sums r=-.47 (balanced) and r=-.33 (unbalanced). After control F=0.00 and F=0.04.
limits: Lab task with learned symptom-disease frequencies, not real clinicians. Mediation by statistical control, not manipulation.
agent_relevance: Supports counting generated hypotheses as a leading indicator of overconfidence and prompting for breadth before judging.

source: Dougherty and Hunter (2003) Hypothesis generation, probability judgment, and individual differences in working memory capacity (Acta Psychologica 113:263-282)
finding: Lower working memory capacity people behaved as if they kept fewer hypotheses in mind and gave higher, more subadditive probabilities (as summarised by Thomas et al. 2014).
numbers: No numbers read. Bibliographic confirmation from search results only.
limits: Not opened. Companion paper Memory and Cognition 31:968-982 (2003a).
agent_relevance: Individual differences in capacity are a human-specific moderator. For an LLM the analogue is context budget and what is written down.

source: Mehle (1980) Hypothesis generation in an automobile malfunction inference task (PhD dissertation, University of Oklahoma)
finding: Expert and novice subjects both had trouble producing complete hypothesis sets and were overconfident in the probabilities of their sets.
numbers: Abstract only; no N or rates seen.
limits: Dissertation abstract only. No 1982 journal version found in search.
agent_relevance: Original human evidence that listed hypotheses feel more complete than they are. Matches b01 to b03.

source: Mehle, Gettys, Fisher et al. (1980) DTIC final report on hypothesis generation 1977-1980
finding: Report concludes that failure to retrieve enough hypotheses and a belief that the retrieved set is more complete than it is trace to deficits in memory retrieval.
numbers: No numbers: the PDF returned HTTP 403, and only a search-snippet summary was seen.
limits: Not opened. Summary comes from a search snippet.
agent_relevance: Names the cause as retrieval, not reasoning. Retrieval prompts (cues, category sweeps) are the lever.

source: Elstein, Shulman, Sprafka (1978) Medical Problem Solving, via search snippets (JFP 1980 article, a patent text, Sprafka 1973 thesis)
finding: Physicians form hypotheses very early. A 1980 Journal of Family Practice article reports a McMaster follow-up found no difference between family physicians and internists in number or type of hypotheses.
numbers: A patent states a mean of 2 to 4 hypotheses held at once (unverified, unattributed). Sprafka 1973 thesis classed subjects as using many or few hypotheses (snippet is inconsistent: '3-10' vs '<10').
limits: Unverified second-hand numbers. The 2 to 4 count could not be checked against the 1978 book.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code a number like four from this. Only the early-generation pattern is secure.

source: Weber, Boeckenholt, Hilton, Wallace (1993) Determinants of diagnostic hypothesis generation: effects of information, base rates, and experience (JEP:LMC 19:1151)
finding: Order and frequency of generated hypotheses followed the amount of supporting information and population base rates, with little base rate neglect. Having diagnosed a similar case earlier made that diagnosis come up earlier and more often. Experience acted only by raising the availability of similar cases.
numbers: Abstract only. No N or effect sizes seen.
limits: Abstract only. Physicians, written case histories.
agent_relevance: Cues drive generation through similarity to stored cases. Priming with a similar earlier case is a risk for an LLM that sees earlier examples in context.

source: Kostopoulou et al. (2016) The role of physicians' first impressions in the diagnosis of possible cancers without alarm symptoms (Medical Decision Making)
finding: A first impression that mentioned cancer predicted the later diagnosis. Asking more cancer-related questions mediated part of this.
numbers: 90 UK family physicians, 6 cases, 297 coded verbalizations (kappa .89). Odds of diagnosing cancer 4.90 times higher (95% CI 2.72-8.84), referral odds 1.98 (1.10-3.57). Mediation by cancer questions 29 percent of the total effect.
limits: Abstract only (full PDF not retrieved). Association, not manipulation: first impressions may reflect case features.
agent_relevance: Quantifies how much the first hypothesis steers search. A cheap first hypothesis must be treated as a search director, not just a guess.

source: Mamede et al. (2010) Effect of availability bias and reflective reasoning on diagnostic accuracy among internal medicine residents (JAMA 304:1198)
finding: Prior exposure to similar cases lowered second-year residents' accuracy on look-alike cases; reflection restored accuracy.
numbers: N=36 residents (18 first-year, 18 second-year). Second-years scored 1.55 on look-alike cases vs 2.19 on others (P=.03); first-years showed the opposite pattern (2.03 vs 1.42, P=.046). Biased phase-1 diagnosis given 1.44 vs 0.72 per resident (P=.04). Reflection raised accuracy (second-years 1.55 to 2.03; first-years to 2.31).
limits: Abstract and snippets only. Small N, interaction with training year, reflection phase always came last (order confound) and extra time was not controlled.
agent_relevance: Primary evidence that a structured re-analysis step can undo bias from a primed hypothesis. Order and time are uncontrolled, so size is uncertain.

source: Staal et al. (2021) Relationship between time to diagnose and diagnostic accuracy among internal medicine residents: a randomized experiment (BMC Med Educ)
finding: Tried to reproduce Mamede-style availability bias induction in 117 residents and failed. Correct diagnoses came faster than incorrect ones, so 'slow down' is not obviously the fix.
numbers: N=117 residents (113 analysed), multi-centre, within-subject. No significant bias effect. Correct 115 s vs incorrect 129 s (t(112)=4.51, p<.001, d=0.37). Confidence-accuracy fit R2=0.03. Residents wanted extra resources in 63 percent of cases. Planned N 128 for a medium effect.
limits: Failed induction means bias errors could not be analysed alone. Exploratory: bias errors resembled correct diagnoses in time (115 vs 115 s) and were faster than other errors (136 s, p=.082).
agent_relevance: A failed replication of the induction effect: availability bias in vignettes is less robust than the famous result suggests. Do not make 'slow down' a blanket rule.

source: Mamede et al. (2020) 'Immunising' physicians against availability bias in diagnostic reasoning: a randomised controlled experiment (BMJ Qual Saf 29:550)
finding: Knowledge that separates look-alike diseases, taught with contrasting cases and feedback, reduced bias. Process-focused debiasing had mostly failed before.
numbers: 91 second-year residents in 8 Brazilian hospitals. On biased vignettes immunised 0.40 vs non-immunised 0.24 (difference 0.16, 95% CI 0.05-0.27, p=.004). On non-biased vignettes 0.36 vs 0.41 (p=.45).
limits: Abstract only. Simulated setting; measured one week later; two disease clusters only.
agent_relevance: Supports giving the agent discriminating features for confusable pairs (contrast knowledge), not just a rule to consider alternatives.

source: Interventions to improve diagnostic decision making: a systematic review and meta-analysis on reflective strategies (Medical Teacher, 2019)
finding: Guided reflection improved diagnostic decisions. Other strategies (checklists, debiasing workshops, instructions for analytical thinking) could not be pooled.
numbers: 44 studies from 10,114 screened, 4380 professionals. Guided reflection effect size 0.38 (95% CI 0.23-0.52), p<0.001.
limits: Abstract only; author list not checked. Pooled only for reflection; study quality limited.
agent_relevance: Best pooled number for a structured re-analysis step. Moderate size, not large.

source: Effect on diagnostic accuracy of cognitive reasoning tools for the workplace setting: systematic review and meta-analysis (BMJ Qual Saf 2022;31:899)
finding: Tools meant to improve clinical reasoning gave a small gain in diagnostic accuracy.
numbers: 29 studies, 2732 participants. Hedges g=0.20 (95% CI 0.10-0.29), p<0.001, after removing 3 studies with tool training (I2 70 percent fell to 38 percent). No subgroup differences found.
limits: Abstract only. Heterogeneity was large before exclusions. No moderator explained larger gains.
agent_relevance: Realistic ceiling for scaffold-type reasoning aids is small (g about 0.2). Do not expect big jumps from a checklist alone.

source: Norman et al. (2017) The causes of errors in clinical reasoning: cognitive biases, knowledge deficits, and dual process thinking (Academic Medicine)
finding: Biases, especially availability, can be induced in the lab but their share of real errors is not established. Teaching bias recognition does not reduce errors, while knowledge reorganisation gives small but consistent gains.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Rival explanation: errors from knowledge gaps rather than bias. A scaffold that only says 'avoid bias' may miss the main error source.

source: Sherbino et al. (2014) Ineffectiveness of cognitive forcing strategies to reduce biases in diagnostic reasoning: a controlled trial (CJEM)
finding: Training medical students in cognitive forcing strategies did not reduce diagnostic error.
numbers: 191 students (145 trained, 46 control). Search-satisficing cases: 52 vs 48 percent started a search for a second diagnosis (p=.91); 54 vs 48 percent found it (p=.13). Availability cases: 45 percent in both groups found the uncommon diagnosis (p=.98).
limits: Abstract only. Novices; unequal groups. A 2011 exploratory study (n=56) found poor application and retention.
agent_relevance: Null result for 'remember to think of a second diagnosis' training. Telling is not enough; the second search has to be built into the procedure.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large language model influence on diagnostic reasoning: a randomized clinical trial (medRxiv preprint; JAMA Network Open version)
finding: Giving physicians GPT-4 did not improve their diagnostic reasoning, although GPT-4 alone scored much higher than the physicians.
numbers: 50 physicians (26 attending, 24 resident), 5.2 cases each, 60 minutes. Median score 76.3 percent with GPT-4 vs 73.7 conventional; adjusted difference 1.6 points (95% CI -4.4 to 7.6, p=.60). Time 519 s vs 565 s. GPT-4 alone median 92.1; difference to conventional group 15.5 points (95% CI 1.5-29.5, p=.03).
limits: Preprint text read; journal version may differ. One chatbot, vignettes, no training in prompt use. The rubric rewards listing differentials with findings for and against.
agent_relevance: A supplied strong differential did not transfer to the human. The model's own list is strong, so use it, but test whether supplied hypotheses get used or ignored.

source: McDuff et al. (2025) Towards accurate differential diagnosis with large language models (Nature)
finding: A diagnosis-tuned LLM gave better differentials than unassisted clinicians, and clinicians assisted by it had more comprehensive lists than clinicians with search.
numbers: 20 clinicians, 302 case reports. Standalone top-10 accuracy 59.1 vs 33.6 percent for unassisted (P=0.04). Assisted arms: 51.7 percent with LLM vs 36.1 unassisted and 44.4 with search.
limits: Abstract only. Case-report text, not live encounters. Differs from b22 (no human gain); outcomes differ (list accuracy vs reasoning score).
agent_relevance: Supplied hypotheses raised list breadth for humans here. The two trials disagree, depending on the outcome measured.

source: Ke et al. (2024) Enhancing diagnostic accuracy through multi-agent conversations: using LLMs to mitigate cognitive bias (arXiv 2401.14589)
finding: A GPT-4 team with a devil's advocate and a facilitator agent recovered the right diagnosis in cases chosen because clinicians had been misled by anchoring and premature closure.
numbers: 16 case reports (15 published plus 1 unpublished), 80 simulations. Initial diagnosis 0/80 correct; top differential 57/80 (71.3 percent); final two differentials 64/80 (80.0 percent). Kappa .838 for repeated runs of top diagnosis. 13 of 16 scenarios reached the correct diagnosis.
limits: No single-agent control and no unbiased cases: initial accuracy is 0 by case selection, and cases may be in training data. The roles combine two changes (more agents, explicit bias roles).
agent_relevance: Suggests a rival-hypothesis role helps, but not that it beats one agent asked for a differential. A control arm is needed before we copy it.

source: Handler, Bedi, Shah (2026) Quantifying and mitigating premature closure in frontier LLMs (arXiv 2605.15000), multiple choice with the right option removed
finding: Five frontier models picked an answer when the correct option had been removed. A safety prompt that allows abstention cut this but did not remove it.
numbers: MedQA n=500 (250 intact, 250 no-correct-option), AfriMed-QA n=490. False action about 70 percent at baseline, about 48 percent with safety prompt. MedQA by model: Claude Opus 4.7 81 to 65, GPT-5.4 64 to 42, Grok 3 75 to 29, Gemini 2.5 Pro 55 to 48, DeepSeek R1 78 to 53. Intact accuracy fell about 1.0 point (excluding Grok 3).
limits: LLM judges scored open-ended items; one simple prompt; model names as reported in the preprint. Grok 3 traded accuracy for abstention.
agent_relevance: Direct measure of premature commitment in LLMs. A stop-and-check prompt buys about 20 points and leaves about half of failures.

source: Handler, Bedi, Shah (2026) premature closure in open-ended HealthBench items
finding: Models committed to answers most when a question was under-specified but looked low risk, and handled urgency cues better than missing context. Adversarial prompts broke all models.
numbers: HealthBench subset n=861: baseline premature closure 73.2 percent (GPT-5.4) to 96.1 percent (DeepSeek R1) on under-specified low-risk items; overall 20.7 to 44.6 percent; safety prompt cut overall by 4.2 to 7.9 points. Adversarial n=191: 59.3 percent (Claude Opus 4.7) to 91.4 percent (DeepSeek R1) at baseline; lowest residual 50.8 percent. Sufficient-context control: clarification rate 3.5 percent, so no broad over-deferral.
limits: LLM-based judging with rubrics; single simple prompt. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Models react to risk cues, not to missing information. The scaffold needs an explicit missing-information check (what would change my answer) because urgency cues will not trigger it.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models (npj Digit Med 7:295)
finding: Bias-inducing text added to USMLE questions lowered accuracy in six LLMs; GPT-4 was the most robust.
numbers: BiasMedQA: 1273 questions, seven biases. Baseline accuracy GPT-4 72.7 percent, Mixtral 51.8, GPT-3.5 49.7, PMC-Llama-13B 33.4. Drops of 10 to 26 percent depending on bias; GPT-4 worst case about 14.0 percent under false consensus and 0.2 percent (p=.91) under confirmation. Some models dropped 50 percent or more.
limits: Biases were injected through prompt wording, which differs from a model forming its own early hypothesis. Multiple-choice format. About 5.3 percent of questions may lack enough information.
agent_relevance: Shows suggestible context lowers accuracy, i.e. anchoring on supplied framing. Measures prompt anchors, not self-generated anchoring.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) BiasMedQA mitigation results
finding: A bias warning, one-shot and few-shot bias demonstrations gave small gains. GPT-4 gained most from few-shot examples; weaker models sometimes refused or produced nonsense.
numbers: GPT-4 best average 75.2 percent with few-shot; Recency accuracy 0.679 to 0.742 with one-shot. GPT-3.5 +6.1 percent (education, p<1e-16), +4.3 one-shot, +5.2 few-shot. Mixtral best with education, average 48.4 percent. PaLM-2 non-response 94.4 percent (one-shot) and 99.5 percent (few-shot).
limits: Improved but did not restore baseline accuracy. Gains depend on model capability. Safety filters distorted PaLM-2.
agent_relevance: Simple warnings give only a few points. Worked examples help strong models, which fits the human result that process warnings do little (b21).

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster, arXiv 2403.00811)
finding: Tested anchoring, status quo, framing, group attribution and primacy in admissions decisions. Self-help debiasing helped for prompt-induced bias, and few-shot examples sometimes broke the model.
numbers: 13,465 prompts. Llama models changed 40 to 52 percent of earlier decisions when asked to debias themselves (over-correction). Self-help cut biased prompts in framing and status quo to 17.2 and 8.5 percent.
limits: Non-medical task; anchoring here means influence of the model's earlier decisions, which differs from diagnostic anchoring. Effects mostly small.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: self-debiasing can over-correct and flip good answers. Any re-check step needs a rule for when to hold the original answer.

source: Mahajan, Obermeyer, Daneshjou, Lester, Powell (2025) Cognitive bias in clinical large language models (npj Digit Med News and Views)
finding: Commentary claims LLMs anchor because autoregressive text gives more weight to earlier-formed hypotheses, and that structured prompts can reduce this. It cites Ke et al. for anchoring on a wrong first diagnosis and a two-step summarise-then-differential prompt for radiology.
numbers: No new data. Cited: Ke 2024 (b24); a Sonoda 2024 preprint reporting a two-step prompt reduced anchoring (no figures in this piece); a pathology study where experts kept wrong estimates when an LLM agreed.
limits: Commentary, not an experiment. The autoregression mechanism is stated, not tested. Acknowledges reliance on vignettes.
agent_relevance: Pointer to the two-step prompt idea (findings first, differential second). Treat the mechanism as a hypothesis until measured.

source: Information-seeking failures of large language models in agentic clinical reasoning (arXiv 2607.10275)
finding: In a hematology-oncology task with three rounds of data requests, 32 frontier models showed search satisficing, anchoring and premature closure. Reasoning quality did not track accuracy.
numbers: Best model 68 percent accuracy. Information utilization vs accuracy R=0.69 (P<0.001). Utilization fell from 57 to 26 percent in the final round. 91 percent of traces scored above the rubric threshold, with no correlation to accuracy.
limits: Only the abstract page was seen; model names and methods not checked. Single domain.
agent_relevance: What matters is gathering data, not writing a fluent rationale. Track information coverage as a signal, not rationale quality.
